route.start: Marine Drive (Princess Street flyover), Mumbai, Maharashtra

timeline.event: Both tunnels under Malabar Hill are holed through by the tunnel boring machine

Fully open round-the-clock; the 7.5 km seaside promenade opens in August

history: South Mumbai is a narrow finger of land with only two roads running up it, so for decades a trip from Marine Drive to Worli in the evening rush could take the best part of an hour. Mumbai's Coastal Road is the city's answer: a new expressway along the western shoreline, built partly on land reclaimed from the sea and partly in twin tunnels bored under Malabar Hill. It was built by the city's own municipal corporation, the BMC, rather than by a state or national agency, which is unusual for a project this size. Construction started in 2018; the southbound side opened in March 2024, the northbound side later that year, and the whole road was running round the clock by 2025. At the Worli end it joins the Bandra–Worli Sea Link, so traffic can carry straight on toward the western suburbs. Just as importantly, the reclaimed land was not all given to cars — a long public promenade, parks and open space were built beside the road and opened in 2025.
facts: Its twin tunnels pass beneath Girgaum Chowpatty and Malabar Hill — often described as India's first undersea road tunnels.
Each tunnel is about 2.07 km long; they were dug by 'Mavala', one of the largest tunnel boring machines ever used in India.
Cuts the Marine Drive–Worli drive to around 10 minutes, from close to an hour in the evening rush.
Comes with a new public promenade, parks and green space built along the reclaimed shoreline.
Interchanges at Amarsons Garden, Breach Candy, Haji Ali and Worli let drivers join and leave the road.
Underground car parks built beneath the new open spaces hold roughly 1,850 vehicles in total.
It was built by the BMC, the city's municipal corporation — one of the biggest road projects any Indian city government has built on its own.
significance: The Coastal Road is the first genuinely new north–south route south Mumbai has had in generations, and it takes thousands of cars a day off Marine Drive, Peddar Road and the Worli seaface. It also changed what Mumbaikars expect from a big road project: instead of only lanes, it delivered a wide public promenade, cycle track and gardens on reclaimed land, which is now the template for the northern phase. Together with the Atal Setu and the Eastern Freeway, it is part of the ring of fast roads the city is knitting around its harbour and coastline.

travelNotes: Marine Drive to Worli takes roughly 10 to 12 minutes, and there is no toll. The busiest flows are northbound in the evening and southbound in the morning, when office traffic reverses. The tunnels are the quickest bit but also where breakdowns cause the worst jams, so keep your distance. The promenade alongside is a favourite evening walk and gets crowded at sunset and on weekends, so expect people and parked cars near the access points.
futureUpgrades: A northern extension along the coast, from Versova through Dahisar to Bhayandar, is being built by the BMC.
MMRDA is boring twin tunnels from Orange Gate on the Eastern Freeway to Marine Drive, due around 2028, which will connect the Coastal Road directly to Mumbai's eastern side.
A long sea-facing promenade is planned along the northern phase, extending the one already open in the south.
